title: The Godot Course, Sketched
rules: The order is the Ada spine: its 25 sequences, one chapter each; you learn programming by building the Ada examples of that sequence's halls.

Part I (sequences 1 to 5) climbs the Learning Processing ladder (Shiffman) in Godot 4.6 and GDScript: shapes and coordinates, flow, interaction, variables, conditionals, loops, functions, objects, arrays. A concept is used only after it is taught; a part a hall needs earlier is supplied and named as borrowed.
From sequence 6 (change) on, the content is The Nature of Code (Shiffman) in the spine's order; shaders, isosurfaces, boolean surfaces, graph theory and the last three sequences are Ada's own.

The voice is The Nature of Code's: second person, friendly, exact, as little text as possible. One idea per short numbered section, a picture for every idea, the code, a sentence or two of why; numbered examples, a few exercises, one running project.
Build from the ground up: each chapter uses only what came before. Haeckel's radiolaria and other specific forms are case studies for later, noted as hooks.

Godot 4.6, GDScript, desktop first, the headset where a hall is about being held or walked. The course look: hot pink sky, violet ground, acid lime body, cyan, orange, off-white, lavender for what has no collider.
running_project: One running project goes through the whole book: your room, and a figure you make yourself (after Learning Processing's Zoog). The figure is composed from Godot's shapes (1), moves and decides (2), stands on a floor of copies (3), becomes a class (4) and is kept in an array and dressed in a pattern (5). Then it is thrown (6), becomes a Mover that forces push (7), gets a net hung over it and a marble (8), and swings and rings (9). It wanders by seeded chance (10), climbs a noise hill (11), wears a computed skin (12), climbs a Rule 90 stair (13) and walks through a Menger sponge (14). It keeps a garden, a family of plants grown by one rule with different genes (15), and enters a world bred from one seed (16). It walks through a soft curtain (17), stands in a doorway cut from a field (18) and from solids (19), and is copied into a flock (20). It learns (21), finds its way through the room's graph (22), stands where an impossible body closes (23) and is wired to the laboratory's handles (24). In 25 the room is released with one body any visitor can change.

parts.title: Coding with Bodies
parts.summary: Part I teaches programming from nothing, using the first five spine sequences. Each sequence takes the next rungs of the Learning Processing ladder, in order. Primitives (ch1) opens with how to make a script and press Play, then teaches shapes and coordinates, flow, interaction and variables. Transformation (ch2) teaches conditionals. array_tutorial (ch3) teaches loops. Color (ch4) teaches functions, then objects. Tiling (ch5) teaches arrays. Every chapter builds the main examples of its halls with only what came before. Where a hall needs something earlier, a small supplied part does the job and is named as borrowed. The running project is My Room: a figure you make yourself (Learning Processing's Zoog). It is composed from Godot's shapes, then moves and decides, then stands on a floor of copies, then becomes a class with colour functions, and is finally kept in an array and dressed in a pattern.

parts.title: Motion
parts.summary: Part II opens The Nature of Code. You already have the whole ladder from Part I; now things start to move. Chapter 6 starts with velocity and acceleration (NOC 1), then reads a rate and a sum out of the same steps, and ends on a field that tells a particle where to go next. Chapter 7 opens the vector itself (add, dot, length) and builds a Mover class that wind, drag, a spring and an attractor push around; it ends with a place that has its own gravity (NOC 1 and 2). Chapter 8 lets rules settle into forms: a point walks downhill, a net of Particles relaxes into a hanging form that turns over into a vault, arms balance, and an annealer climbs out of small valleys (NOC 6). Chapter 9 turns the circle sideways into a sine and follows what returns: a pendulum, its swing laid out across the floor, sine surfaces, travelling waves, a tone computed sample by sample, and sums of waves (NOC 3). Each chapter adds one thing to your figure and your room: a launch, a Mover with a corner of its own gravity, a hung-and-inverted vault, and something that returns.

Chapter 12 is Ada's own: the same shaping, noise and octaves move onto the GPU, where they become a skin computed for every pixel. It ends with a buffer that gives the rule a past, which is the door into cellular automata.

parts.title: Growth
parts.summary: Four chapters where small rules, repeated, grow large forms. Cellular automata (NOC 7): a cell reads its neighbours, and the history becomes a floor you stand on. Fractals (NOC 8.1-8.5): a function calls itself, and trees, dust, snowflakes and a sponge you walk into come out of one line. L-systems (NOC 8.6): a sentence is rewritten and a turtle reads it, so a string becomes a plant, a corridor, or a family of faces. Procedural generation (NOC 9, plus Ada's own): bodies are bred by a score, trees grow toward food, rooms are carved, and patterns are copied, all from one seed. Each chapter builds only on what came before it: two buffers (13), then recursion (14), then strings and stacks (15), then populations and search (16). Case studies (Turing, Haeckel, Conway, Sims) are noted as hooks for later.

sections.title: A number for every place

sections.figure: A 10 x 10 x 10 lattice of white dots, iso view, each dot sized by its noise value.

sections.title: A level makes a boundary
sections.idea: Pick one number: samples above it are inside, below it outside, and the boundary runs between.
sections.figure: One field of three sources cut at 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8, front view: one body, one body, three, three smaller.

sections.title: Eight corners, one case

parts.title: Beyond
parts.summary: Part VI starts with bodies that learn: NOC 10 neural networks, framed by NOC 11 neuroevolution and the return of Chapter 16's genetic algorithm. Next comes graph theory: connections you can search, draw, cross, cut and pair. Then Ada's own ending. The crisis of foundations builds bodies that the rules you have used cannot hold. The QFEP laboratory takes Ada's formula apart into four handles and wires them to bodies. Post-crisis computing turns every earlier tool back on the room: who it lets in, what it keeps, who may change it. The running project, My Room, ends here, released to desktop and headset with a guest any visitor can change.

sections.title: A learner with no teacher

sections.figure: Two populations from above: bodies drifting over energy cells with their trails, and a scored population whose best are copied each generation.

sections.title: Error is a height
sections.idea: Every line through your points has an error, so draw the error as a height over slope and intercept and you get a landscape.
sections.figure: The squared-error bowl over a floor whose axes are slope and intercept, one candidate line marked as a lime point on it.

sections.title: Walk downhill
sections.idea: Nudge each number, see which way the error falls and step that way: that is gradient descent.
sections.figure: Top view of the bowl with two trails of steps: small steps curving into the bottom, large steps overshooting back and forth.
sections.caption: The step size is the learning rate.

sections.title: Centres that move
sections.idea: Give each point to its nearest centre, move each centre to the middle of its points and repeat until nothing changes.
sections.figure: Three frames from above: random centres, the first colouring, the settled centres with their coloured points.

sections.title: The perceptron
